identity.title: Integrative Genomic and Stem Cell Frameworks for Variant-to-Function Discovery in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Narrative Review.

content.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a heterogeneous neurodevelopmental condition shaped by de novo protein-truncating variants, inherited missense substitutions, recurrent copy number variations (CNVs), and distributed polygenic risk. These alterations converge on a limited set of neurobiological processes, including synaptic refinement, excitation-to-inhibition balance, chromatin state regulation, and glial-mediated neuroimmune signaling. Experimental paradigms now exist for systematic variant-to-function interrogation through CRISPR-engineered isogenic human pluripotent stem-cell libraries incorporating Cas9 nucleases, programmable transcriptional modulators (dCas9-KRAB and dCas9-VP64), base editors, and prime editing systems. Coupled with single-cell multi-omic platforms such as Perturb-seq, scATAC-seq, and CITE-seq, and with circuit-level phenotyping through multielectrode arrays, calcium imaging, and quantitative morphometry, these systems resolve ASD-relevant cellular states at single-cell and cell-type-specific resolution. In this narrative review, we distinguish deliberately between what these platforms have already established and what remains proposed. To date, a small number of studies constitute the demonstrated evidence base: in vivo Perturb-seq of 35 ASD/neurodevelopmental risk genes in mouse cortex, mosaic knockout of ASD genes in human cortical organoids, the CHOOSE organoid screen of 36 risk genes, assembloid CRISPR screening of 425 neurodevelopmental-disorder risk genes, a 63-line mouse embryonic stem-cell CNV resource, and a CRISPRi screen of 102 ASD risk genes in human induced pluripotent stem-cell (iPSC)-derived microglia implicating ADNP in synaptic pruning. We summarized these in a dedicated comparison table. Against this, integration of polygenic and noncoding architecture, causal-inference frameworks, such as Mendelian randomization and do-calculus, and cross-laboratory reproducibility, remain aspirational rather than realized. We therefore frame the field's principal near-term requirement not as further gene discovery but as harmonized protocols, shared reference lines, arrayed validation capacity, and interpretable statistical frameworks capable of converting perturbation atlases into causal mechanism.
